analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits for low earners, students, and widows, paid for with a new payroll tax on income above $250,000.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to four House committees in 2019 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would increase Social Security benefits in several ways: it would raise benefits for people who worked many years at low wages up to at least the poverty level, extend child benefits to full-time students through age 22, use a cost-of-living index that tracks older consumers' spending, and give widows and widowers in two-income households a higher benefit. To pay for it, the bill would apply the Social Security payroll tax to wages and self-employment income above $250,000 a year, which are currently untaxed above about $137,700. It would also make sure higher benefits don't cause people to lose SSI, Medicaid, or CHIP eligibility.
analysis.who_benefits: Lifetime low earners get a new minimum benefit scaled to years worked, reaching 125% of the poverty guideline for 30 years of work. Children of retired, disabled, or deceased workers who are full-time college students could keep benefits until 23 instead of 19. All beneficiaries would get cost-of-living increases based on the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which typically runs higher than the standard index. Widows and widowers in two-income households would get a supplemental benefit. People on SSI, Medicaid, or CHIP would be protected from losing benefits because of the higher Social Security payments.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-earning retirees, disabled workers, students, and widows

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a minimum Social Security benefit for lifetime low earners, scaled from 6.25% to 125% of the annual poverty guideline based on years of work, with recomputation for people already receiving benefits.

Extends child benefits to full-time students through age 22 (the current cutoff is 19 for secondary school), including college students, and applies the same change to the Railroad Retirement program.
Switches cost-of-living adjustments to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers (CPI-E), which tracks the spending patterns of older consumers, typically producing larger annual increases.
Gives widows and widowers in two-income households an alternative benefit of 75% of the combined household benefits, capped by a formula, instead of choosing only one spouse's benefit.
Holds SSI, Medicaid, and CHIP beneficiaries harmless by disregarding any increase in Social Security benefits above the pre-enactment amount when determining eligibility for those programs.
Pays for the benefit increases by applying Social Security payroll taxes to earnings above $250,000, which is currently exempt above the taxable maximum ($137,700 for 2020).

analysis.who_pays: Workers and self-employed people earning more than $250,000 a year, plus their employers, would pay Social Security payroll taxes on income above that level for the first time. The bill includes a small offset: 2% of earnings above $250,000 would count toward the payer's own benefit formula. Earnings between the current cap (about $137,700) and $250,000 would remain untaxed, preserving the current treatment for upper-middle earners.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above $250,000 and their employers

drawbacks.text: The tax creates a 'donut hole': earnings between the current taxable maximum and $250,000 remain untaxed, so the tax lands only on the very highest earners and the bill leaves the current gap untouched for everyone else.
High earners and their employers face a new tax on income above $250,000, and employers of high-paid workers bear the employer share, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.

The bill gives high earners a small return on the new taxes: 2% of earnings above $250,000 counts in the benefit formula, which slightly reduces the amount available to fund the benefit increases for others.

Using the CPI-E for cost-of-living adjustments raises benefits faster each year than the current index, increasing program spending growth permanently, though the bill does not say where that cost beyond the new tax is covered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets benefit increases at the groups with the smallest checks — lifetime low earners, widows, students — and pays for them with a tax that affects only the top slice of earners, while protecting SSI and Medicaid recipients from indirect losses. The design is deliberate and well-aimed, though the CPI-E change grows program costs permanently and the benefit formula gives some of the new tax revenue back to the high earners paying it. The main reason it did not advance was not a flaw in the design but a lack of legislative traction: four cosponsors and no committee action in 17 months.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in four House committees and their subcommittees from July 2019 until the Congress ended in January 2021, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Al Lawson of Florida introduced the bill on July 30, 2019, joined by Reps. Norton, Tlaib, and Wilson of Florida as original cosponsors.

The House referred it to four committees — Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Energy and Commerce — and then to subcommittees on Social Security, Health, and Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials.
No committee or subcommittee took further action, and the bill received no vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill had 4 cosponsors, all House Democrats, out of 231 House Democrats in that Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People earning more than $250,000 a year are better off because the bill died: they would have paid Social Security payroll taxes above $250,000 for the first time, and no other funding source replaced it. Low-earning beneficiaries, students, and widows are in the same position as before — no benefit increases.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners who would have paid the new tax

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored and cosponsored exclusively by Democrats, and no Republican or Democratic action on the bill ever appears in the record; the bill simply never moved, so no vote split exists to measure.

industries.note: The bill would subject wages and self-employment income above $250,000 to Social Security payroll taxes for the first time, with only a small 2% benefit-formula credit in return. Because the bill died, these households continue to pay no Social Security tax above the roughly $137,700 cap.
The employer share of the payroll tax would apply to wages above $250,000, raising labor costs for firms paying top salaries. The bill's death leaves those costs unchanged.
Lifetime low earners, student children, and widows and widowers would have received larger checks, with SSI, Medicaid, and CHIP eligibility protected. None of these increases happened.
